sections.heading: The Snapchat tradeoff
sections.content: Butterfield described watching a teenager tap four to six times per second for about six minutes as she moved through stories, replayed or skipped them, switched people, answered a notification, and took a selfie. Despite the high tap count, the experience felt fluid and matched what she wanted from Snapchat. He argued that trying to make her tap less could have impeded the experience she and Snapchat wanted to create.

sections.heading: Design principle
sections.content: The point is not to minimize taps at any cost, but to make actions trivially easy and avoid forcing users to think through difficult choices. Butterfield said even eight easy taps can be preferable to two taps that require navigating menus and weighing options.

sections.heading: The tradeoff
sections.content: Butterfield watched a teenager tap at least four times per second—sometimes six or seven—for about six minutes while moving fluidly among stories, people, and other actions. He argued that trying to make her tap less could have impeded the experience she and Snapchat wanted. The broader principle is that fewer taps are not automatically simpler: several trivially easy steps can be preferable to fewer taps that force users into difficult decisions or comparisons.
